Invalid JSON when parsing {"candidates":[{"candidate_id":"cnsms2026-a1","title":"Empirical evaluation of generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipelines versus LLM-only and traditional automation for intent-to-configuration NetOps tasks","research_question":"Does a generate–validate–repair pipeline (LLM generation + deterministic network verifier + automated repair loop) produce network configurations that satisfy operator intent and formal safety properties more reliably than LLM-only generation and traditional scripted automation under a shared task set?","hypotheses":["A GVR pipeline will produce a higher proportion of configurations that pass deterministic verification (reachability/policy checks) than LLM-only generation.","GVR will produce fewer unsafe or policy-violating configurations executed on simulated devices than LLM-only generation.","GVR will match or exceed traditional scripted automation on verification pass-rate while reducing required human intervention time per task."],"proposed_design":"Preregistered, controlled experiment using a public/synthesized corpus of N=300 high-level NetOps intents mapped to device templates and topology models. Three arms: (1) LLM-only: single-shot LLM prompt to produce device configs; (2) GVR: LLM-generated config -> Batfish-style verifier (or equivalent deterministic verifier) -> automated repair prompts and up to 3 repair iterations; (3) Traditional automation baseline: template-based/config-generator scripts (idempotent templates). Each produced config is evaluated by the deterministic verifier for reachability, ACL/policy compliance, and loop/blackhole introduction. Execute configs in a sandboxed network simulator to detect runtime failures. Record verification pass/fail, number of repair iterations, human-intervention proxy (operator review needed), and end-to-end latency. All prompts, model seeds, verifier runs, and simulator logs are preserved. Randomize intent assignment to arms and use paired comparisons where feasible.","expected_data":"Per-arm dataset of 300 tasks (900 total attempts), for each attempt: verification result (pass/fail), number of verification-detected violations, number of repair iterations (GVR), simulated-execution outcome (safe/failure), end-to-end latency (ms), and operator-review time proxy. Expect to observe higher verification pass-rate in GVR arm versus LLM-only, and comparable or better pass-rate versus traditional scripts on intent-generalization cases. Anticipate repair iteration distribution skewed low (majority 0–2 iterations).","primary_outcome":"Verification pass-rate per attempted intent (fraction of configs that pass deterministic verifier checks without human modification).","analysis_outline":"Primary comparison: paired proportion tests (McNemar or paired bootstrap) between GVR and LLM-only, and between GVR and traditional automation. Compute 95% confidence intervals for pass-rates. Secondary analyses: logistic regression predicting verification pass (predictors: arm, intent complexity, topology size) and survival analysis for number of repair iterations. Report effect sizes, exact p-values, and corrected multiple comparisons (Benjamini–Hochberg). Provide failure-mode taxonomy and qualitative examples extracted from logs.","novelty_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4413757586","https://openalex.org/W4403443637","https://openalex.org/W4411735779"],"feasibility_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4413757123","https://openalex.org/W4413757586","doi:10.1002/nem.2313"],"risks":["Deterministic verifier may not model all operational behaviors (incomplete oracle) leading to false sense of safety.","Simulated device execution may not capture vendor-specific nuances present in production.","LLM API rate limits or transient failures could bias results if retries are not strictly controlled.","Synthetic intent corpus may not fully represent real operator phrasing, limiting external validity."],"estimated_model_calls":2200},{"candidate_id":"cnsms2026-b2","title":"Limits of LLM-only iterative self-correction on NetOps configuration errors without deterministic verification","research_question":"To what extent can iterative LLM self-correction (multiple self-refinement prompts without an external deterministic verifier) reduce NetOps configuration errors and operational failures, and how susceptible is this process to adversarial or ambiguous inputs?","hypotheses":["Iterative self-correction by an LLM without an external deterministic verifier yields modest improvements in syntactic/formatting errors but limited reduction in semantic safety violations.","Self-correction performance degrades significantly in the presence of adversarially crafted intents or ambiguous device descriptions.","Iterations beyond a small number (e.g., >3) provide diminishing returns and may increase hallucinated but incorrect repairs."],"proposed_design":"Controlled within-subject experiment using N=240 intents across three difficulty strata (simple/template-mapped, moderate intent requiring nontrivial translation, and high-complexity/policy-sensitive). For each task, run: (A) single-shot LLM generation, (B) iterative self-correction loop where the LLM reviews its prior output and attempts repair for up to 4 iterations using only its internal critique and synthesis (no external verifier), and (C) an oracle-augmented GVR (deterministic verifier used) as reference (not part of LLM-only arm). Introduce an adversarial subset (20% of tasks) with prompt-injection or ambiguous topology descriptors. Measure syntactic correctness, semantic policy compliance via an external post-hoc verifier (used only for measurement, not feedback), and simulated execution outcomes. Preserve all outputs and prompts to analyze failure trajectories.","expected_data":"Per-task sequence of generated configs across iterations with post-hoc verifier labels (pass/fail), counts of syntactic vs semantic errors, and simulated-execution safety labels. Subgroup analysis contrasting adversarial vs non-adversarial tasks. Estimate effect sizes and plot learning curves per difficulty stratum. Perform qualitative trajectory analysis on representative success and failure sequences.","novelty_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4403443637","https://openalex.org/W4404534210"],"feasibility_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4413757586","https://openalex.org/W4411735779"],"risks":["Using the post-hoc verifier only for measurement (not feedback) may misrepresent real-world self-correction effectiveness where online feedback could exist.","Adversarial prompt construction may overfit to known attack types and not represent all real-world adversarialities.","Heavy reliance on hosted-model APIs could encounter rate limits or transient behavior changes across runs."],"estimated_model_calls":1500},{"candidate_id":"cnsms2026-c3","title":"NetOps-specific adversarial prompt and artifact robustness: defenses and trade-offs for agentic pipelines","research_question":"How effective are domain-specific input-sanitization and tool-orchestration defenses at reducing successful adversarial manipulations (prompt-injection and malicious intent artifacts) against LLM-driven NetOps pipelines, and what operational latency/cost trade-offs do they introduce?","hypotheses":["NetOps-tailored adversarial inputs significantly increase the rate of unsafe or policy-violating configuration outputs when no defense is present.","Defenses combining input sanitization (structured schema enforcement) and tool-restriction (limiting model tool access) reduce successful adversarial manipulations but increase end-to-end latency and may reduce generalization on benign but atypical operator inputs.","Some lightweight defenses (schema enforcement) offer a favorable latency–security trade-off compared to heavy-weight verifiers for many adversarial cases.",""],"proposed_design":"Adversarial robustness experiment with N=360 tasks, including a curated adversarial corpus of NetOps-formatted attacks (malicious CLI fragments, prompt-injection wrappers, malformed topology descriptions). Evaluate three pipeline defenses: (1) None (baseline LLM-only), (2) Input sanitization: strict schema and token-filtering plus canonicalization before LLM prompt, (3) Tool-orchestration constraint: allow LLM to call only a minimal set of deterministic tools and block free-form outputs; (4) Combined defense (2+3). For each task, measure whether the final produced configuration contains adversarially injected content or results in verification/simulation failure. Measure end-to-end latency per attempt and compute resource/tool calls. Use deterministic verifier for ground-truth labeling and log false-positive defense blocking on benign inputs.","expected_data":"Per-attempt labels: adversarial-success (yes/no), verification pass/fail, latency (ms), defense false-positive rate on benign inputs, and number of tool calls. Anticipate high adversarial-success in baseline, substantial reduction with combined defense, and measurable latency increase (ms to seconds), with input-sanitization showing lower latency cost but higher false-negatives on novel adversarial forms.","primary_outcome":"Adversarial-success rate reduction (fractional decrease in successful adversarial manipulations) relative to baseline for each defense variant.","analysis_outline":"Compare adversarial-success rates across arms using proportion tests (chi-square) with multiple comparisons correction. Model latency–security trade-offs via Pareto analysis and regression (adversarial-success ~ latency + defense type). Report defense false-positive rates and compute receiver operating characteristic for detection components. Provide illustrative attack vectors that bypass each defense and analyze root causes.","novelty_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4406137434","doi:10.2139/ssrn.6956641","https://openalex.org/W4413757586"],"feasibility_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4413757586","https://openalex.org/W4403443637","doi:10.2139/ssrn.6645520"],"risks":["Curated adversarial corpus may not capture future or unseen attack variants, limiting external validity.","Blocking/ sanitization may prevent legitimate operator intents, causing operational friction not fully captured in a simulated experiment.","Defense implementations could interact with specific LLM behavior in a non-generalizable way across model versions."],"estimated_model_calls":1800},{"candidate_id":"cnsms2026-d4","title":"Quantifying verifier-invocation cost versus safety: batching strategies and optimal orchestration in agentic NetOps pipelines","research_question":"How do different verifier-invocation strategies (per-change verification, batched verification, and lazy verification) affect end-to-end safety (verified-correct changes), throughput (changes/sec), and operator latency in agentic NetOps pipelines, and what batching parameters yield optimal safety–latency trade-offs?","hypotheses":["Per-change (immediate) verifier invocation yields the highest verified-correct fraction but lowest throughput and highest latency.","Batched verification (verifying groups of changes) recovers most safety of per-change verification while significantly improving throughput for moderate batch sizes.","There exists an identifiable batching parameter (batch size or time window) that yields a Pareto-optimal trade-off for realistic NetOps workloads.",""],"proposed_design":"Simulation-based orchestration experiment using a workload of N=1000 change requests drawn from a public/synthesized NetOps workload distribution (mix of small template changes and complex intent-driven changes). Implement three orchestration policies: (A) Per-change synchronous verification (invoke verifier for every change), (B) Time-window batching (accumulate for T seconds or up to B changes then run verifier), and (C) Lazy verification (allow immediate simulated execution, verify asynchronously and revert/alert on failures). For each policy and parameter sweep (vary T and B), record verified-correct fraction, throughput (changes/sec), mean operator-observed latency, verifier CPU-time and wall-clock. Use a deterministic verifier for safety labels and simulate rollback costs for failed async executions.","expected_data":"Task-level records for 1000 changes per policy parameterization: verified-correct fraction, throughput, mean and percentile latencies, verifier compute time, and rollback frequency/costs. Expect per-change verification to maximize safety but incur high latency and compute; batching to show diminishing safety loss up to a moderate batch threshold while gaining throughput; lazy verification to show highest throughput but nontrivial rollback costs.","primary_outcome":"Pareto frontier of verified-correct fraction versus mean operator-observed latency (identify batching (T,B) points on the frontier).","analysis_outline":"For each policy/parameter, compute verified-correct fraction and latency; plot Pareto frontiers. Use regression to model verified-correct fraction as a function of batch size and workload mix. Conduct sensitivity analyses across workload mixes and verifier latency distributions. Report compute cost per verified change and expected rollback cost for lazy verification with confidence intervals via bootstrapping.","novelty_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4413757586","doi:10.2139/ssrn.6647800","https://openalex.org/W4413757123"],"feasibility_evidence_ids":["https://openalex.org/W4413757123","https://openalex.org/W4403443637","doi:10.36227/techrxiv.176288195.52086234/v1"],"risks":["Simulated workload may not mirror production workload burstiness, affecting optimal batching estimates.","Verifier runtime variability in real deployments could change trade-offs observed in controlled experiments.","Rollback simulations may under- or over-estimate real operational recovery costs and human intervention delays."],"estimated_model_calls":800}]} for TypeAdapter(CandidateSet); 2 validation errors for CandidateSet
